content: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP) is a liver disorder that occurs during pregnancy, characterized by the accumulation of bile acids in the maternal bloodstream. This condition has been associated with negative outcomes for both the mother and the fetus or neonate. The exact mechanisms underlying ICP are not well understood, and as a result, treatments have largely been based on empirical evidence. Since ICP is relatively rare, with an annual incidence of less than 2%, many clinical trials investigating treatments have been small in scale. However, recent larger trials have provided additional data to guide clinical practice. This review updates previous reviews published in 2001 and 2013. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of pharmacological treatments for ICP on maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes. To achieve this, the authors conducted a comprehensive search of databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth’s Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, up to December 13, 2019. They also reviewed reference lists of relevant studies. The inclusion criteria were randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials, including cluster-randomized trials and trials published in abstract form, that compared any pharmacological treatment with placebo, no treatment, or another drug intervention in women diagnosed with ICP. The review included 26 trials involving a total of 2,007 women. Most of these trials were assessed as having unclear to high risk of bias. The studies evaluated nine different pharmacological interventions, resulting in 14 distinct comparisons. Two placebo-controlled trials of ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) involving 715 women were judged to have a low risk of bias. The pharmacological interventions studied included agents thought to detoxify bile acids (UDCA and S-adenosylmethionine [SAMe]), agents that bind bile acids in the intestine (activated charcoal, guar gum, cholestyramine), Chinese herbal medicines (Yinchenghao decoction [YCHD], Salvia, Yiganling, and Danxioling pill [DXLP]), and agents aimed at reducing bile acid production (dexamethasone). When compared with placebo, UDCA likely results in a modest reduction in pruritus (itching), as measured on a 100 mm visual analogue scale (VAS), where 0 indicates no itching and 100 indicates severe itching. The mean difference in pruritus score was −7.64 points (95% confidence interval [CI] −9.69 to −5.60 points; 2 trials, 715 women; moderate-certainty evidence). However, this reduction in itching may be too small to be considered clinically meaningful for most pregnant women and their healthcare providers. The evidence regarding the effects of UDCA on fetal distress and stillbirth was highly uncertain due to serious limitations in study design and imprecision (risk ratio [RR] 0.70, 95% CI 0.35 to 1.40; 6 trials, 944 women; RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.08 to 1.37; 6 trials, 955 women; very low-certainty evidence). For the other pharmacological interventions included in this review, there were very few differences observed compared to placebo or no treatment. There is insufficient evidence to determine whether SAMe, guar gum, activated charcoal, dexamethasone, cholestyramine, YCHD, DXLP, Salvia, or Yiganling (alone or in combination) are effective in treating ICP. Additionally, no trials have evaluated the efficacy of topical emollients for managing pruritus in ICP. In conclusion, UDCA may provide a small reduction in itching for women with ICP, but the clinical significance of this effect is questionable. The evidence for other adverse fetal outcomes remains unclear due to very low-certainty evidence. There is currently insufficient evidence to support the effectiveness of other pharmacological treatments for ICP. Further high-quality clinical trials are needed to identify effective treatments for maternal itching and to prevent adverse perinatal outcomes. Future research should also aim to identify subgroups of women with ICP who are most likely to benefit from UDCA treatment, such as those with specific bile acid concentration thresholds.
